Q: One aync lock call or multiple async lock calls, what is better and safer in Python? A:

One async lock call is safe. Your code is not safe.

Btw, it is meaningless to have concurrency in the rate limiter of a user. Only meaningful to have concurrency in the part of the business logic of the request. (In case you are trying to make your server slightly faster by sacrificing the strictness of the limit, here's a reminder that releasing and acquiring a lock costs overhead too.)

Your case:

You have four steps which call the same lock:

  • uid_requests.reset_day_limit()
  • uid_requests.exited_day_limit()
  • uid_requests.rate_limited()
  • uid_requests.add_reuqest()

if many requests were sent at the same time, at the period when no one has reached the uid_requests.add_reuqest() step, uid_requests.exited_day_limit() and uid_requests.rate_limited doesn't limit any requests.

Fix:

  1. RateLimiter.on_request:
async def on_request(self) -> tuple[bool, bool]:
    async with self._async_lock:
        current_time_seconds = self.get_now_seconds()

        # check and reset total requests start time as current time seconds
        if self.total_requests_start_time is not None:
            if current_time_seconds - self.total_requests_start_time > self.day_len_seconds:
                self.total_requests_start_time = current_time_seconds
                self.total_requests = 0

        # check exited day limit
        if self.total_requests >= self.max_requests_per_day - 1:
            if self.just_limit_exited:
                self.just_limit_exited = False
                return (True, False)
            return (False, False)

        # check rate limited by last time
        if self.last_time is not None and current_time_seconds - self.last_time < self.seconds_interval:
            if self.just_limit_exited:
                self.just_limit_exited = False
                return (True, False)
            return (False, False)

        # add request with last time as now
        self.last_time = current_time_seconds
        self.just_limit_exited = True
        self.total_requests += 1

        return (False, True)
  1. MainMiddleware.on_request
async def on_request(self, uid: int) -> tuple[bool, bool]:
    uid_requests: RequestsData = self.requsts[uid]
    return await uid_requests.on_request()

Q: Bash Templating: How to build configuration files from templates with Bash? A:

There is another trick that may be useful in some circumstances: prompt expansion with ${var@P}. This expansion does expand some extra \-sequences, but they can even be useful if var represents an informational message. And it's worth mentioning that the most obvious problems of eval can be suppressed with a restricted subshell: $(PATH=; set -r; echo ${var@P}) will disallow command substitution inside var.

Q: How to continuously stream audio from multiple .mp3 files in a sequence into a different .mp3 file? A:

This requires the web server to be specifically made for streaming of media.

You don't "stream" anything into a "file".

Your task is to find a streaming media server. These were popular back in the 90s and 2000s, with the advent of MP3 itself.

Q: Symfony3 Forms: How to know which button was clicked in the form? A:

I encountered the same problem $form->getClickedButton() was always null. The reason was that I had added the Submit-Buttons in the Controller:

$form = $this->createForm(MyEntityType::class, $myentity)
    ->add('save', SubmitType::class, ['label' => 'Save it'])
    ->add('delete', SubmitType::class, ['label' => 'Delete it']);

return $this->render('mytwig.html.twig', ['form' => $form,]);

Very confusing the rendered html contained the two Submit-Buttons but those had no effect. In addition to that adding only one Submit-Button in the Controller worked for me.

The solution is to remove the two Submit-Buttons from the controller and to put them into the FormType instead

class MyEntityType extends AbstractType
{
    public function buildForm(FormBuilderInterface $builder, array $options): void
    {
        $builder
            ->add('name')
            ->add('save', SubmitType::class, ['label' => 'Save it'])
            ->add('delete', SubmitType::class, ['label' => 'Delete it'])
        ;
    }
...

Now $form->getClickedButton() works like a charm in the Controller.

Q: Can a strictly conforming definition of main have argc and argv const-qualified? A:

"Modifiable" and "const" are not opposites of each other. String literals are not const but are not modifiable. Conversely, a const * can point to modifiable data and all you need to do to modify it is cast away constness. Thus, the passage you quote is not relevant to the question of whether the const-adorned main is strictly conforming.

Q: Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s) when dealing with thread in c A:

The version of Valgrind used is too old. You need to use at least version 3.23.

As a rule of thumb, if ever you see a mem* or str* function (or wide char variant) and the top function in the callstack does not refer to vg_replace_strmem.c then the error cannot be relied upon to be accurate. Valgrind needs to be updated to handle that specific string/memory handling function.

Both of the examples produce no errors with recent Valgrind (May 2026, on macOS 13 Intel).
